messages.content: Customer vehicle: 2017 compact sedan, 1.8L four-cylinder, CVT, 172,988 mi. Intermittent no-crank: just a click, and the engine doesn't rotate even a little. The radio and dash stay on and look normal while it clicks. What's the best first check?

reply: [SM 1.4.9] Starter circuit voltage drop test. Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Perform the test with a helper holding the ignition in the start position, measuring voltage drop from the battery positive post to the starter B+ terminal, and from the battery negative post to the engine block. Each side should be under 0.5 V. A higher drop means the starter cannot draw enough current to turn the engine, even when the battery is charged.

snippets.title: Brake fluid moisture test
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2020. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize in the calipers, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination. Take the sample before any fluid is added.

messages.content: I have a 2011 minivan with the 3.5L V6 and the automatic transmission, about 155,304 miles. Cabin heat is weak. The front vents never get properly hot on either side, though the engine seems to warm up fine. Also, highway vibration in the steering wheel starting around 60 mph. It's there whether or not I touch the brakes, and it's smooth at idle. The wipers leave a streak on the driver side. Just tell me what part to replace. I don't need a lesson.

reply:
[cite mode]  
[TSB-6315] Check front caliper slide pins for corrosion or binding while cruising. Pull each slide pin and ensure they move freely by hand.

snippets.title: Pull while cruising from binding caliper slide pins
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with floating front calipers. A pull while cruising may come from a corroded or swollen slide pin that binds and causes uneven pad pressure. Remove each front caliper from its bracket without disconnecting the hose, pull each slide pin and check for corrosion, a swollen boot or binding. Pins should move freely by hand. Repair: clean and lubricate the pins, or fit new pins and boots.

snippets.title: Steering wheel shake at highway speed from wheel imbalance
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2011-2021. A steering wheel shake that peaks in a narrow band such as 60-70 mph may come from tire and wheel assemblies that are out of balance or have high road-force variation. Check each assembly on a road-force balancer. Imbalance should be under 0.25 oz and road-force variation under about 20 lb. Repair: rebalance the assemblies and match-mount as needed.

snippets.title: Heater core inlet and outlet temperature check
snippets.text: Valid for 2010-2015 models. With the engine at operating temperature, the heat set to full hot and the blower on high, measure both heater hoses at the firewall with an infrared thermometer. Both hoses should be hot and within about 15 deg F of each other. A cool outlet hose with a hot inlet indicates restricted flow through the heater core.

messages.content: 2015 compact sedan, 2.0-liter four, automatic, 167,043 miles. The heater only blows lukewarm air from every front vent, even after a 20 minute drive, on both the driver and passenger side. The temperature gauge reads normal.

messages.content: The car pulls hard to the right when I brake. It tracks straight when I'm just driving and when I accelerate. My midsize sedan is a 2014 with the 2.5L, automatic, and 124k on the clock.

reply: [SM 7.5.3] Brake temperature comparison. Apply to 2.5L I4 engine. Park without using the parking brake and measure each front rotor face with an infrared thermometer. Temperatures should be within about 50 deg F side to side. A large difference shows which side is braking harder or dragging. Take both readings within a minute of stopping.

messages.content: My hatchback is a 2016 with the 1.6-liter four, stick shift, and 74k on the clock. The brake pedal feels soft and spongy and goes closer to the floor than it used to, even on the first stop of the day. No warning lights, and no recent brake work. What's the first thing to look at?
Start with this: look at the reservoir level against its marks and at each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
Can't you just tell me what to replace? I'd rather not run tests.
Naming a part now would be a guess. Look at the reservoir level against its marks and at each caliper, hose, line and the master cylinder-to-booster joint for fluid wetness [SEC 11.17].
OK, I tried it. Reservoir is at MAX and there are no wet spots at any wheel or at the master cylinder.
That rules that area out. With the engine off and the booster reserve pumped out, hold steady moderate pressure on the pedal for one minute and watch whether it slowly sinks [SEC 6.4].
Pedal stayed put under steady pressure for the whole minute. OK, so is it the brake line or not? I need a straight answer.

reply: Check the brake fluid moisture content with a test strip or tester [SB 16-592]. If the fluid has more than 3% water, it may be contaminated and could be causing the soft pedal.

snippets.title: Brake fluid moisture test
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2020. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize in the calipers, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination. Take the sample before any fluid is added.

snippets.title: Brake fluid level and leak inspection
snippets.text: Covers 2016-2021 models. Check the master cylinder reservoir level against the MIN and MAX marks. Inspect each caliper, wheel cylinder, brake hose and steel line for wetness, and check the joint between the master cylinder and the brake booster for fluid seepage from the rear seal. Wipe suspect areas clean so fresh seepage is easy to spot.

snippets.title: Pedal that sinks at a stop from master cylinder bypass
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fluid bypassing the master cylinder seals lets the pedal sink slowly at a stop with no external leak. With the engine off, pump the pedal several times to use up booster reserve. Apply steady, moderate pressure and hold it for one minute. Watch the pedal height against a fixed mark. Repair: replace the master cylinder and bleed the system.

snippets.title: Brake fluid moisture test

Take the sample before any fluid is added.

messages.content: Intermittent no-crank: just a click, and the engine doesn't rotate even a little. The radio and dash stay on and look normal while it clicks. Working on a 2019 midsize sedan (2.5-liter four, automatic transmission, 63k miles). What's the best first check?

reply: [TSB-3271] Battery voltage during a start attempt. Connect a meter across the battery posts and watch the reading while a helper attempts to start the engine. Voltage should not fall below 9.6 V. A battery that collapses below that value cannot power the starter and the dashboard lights go dim with the key on.

snippets.title: Click with no crank from the starter control circuit
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with an automatic transmission or CVT, model years 2010-2015. The starter may click or stay silent in park when the range switch, starter relay or wiring drops voltage to the solenoid. Back-probe the solenoid S terminal and have a helper attempt a start in park. The S terminal should see at least 10.5 V during the attempt. Use a back-probe pin so the connector seal is not damaged. Repair: correct the switch, relay or wiring fault.

snippets.title: Battery voltage during a start attempt
snippets.text: Covers 2009-2022 models. Connect a meter across the battery posts and watch the reading while a helper attempts to start the engine. Voltage should not fall below 9.6 V. messages.content: It's a 2013 hatchback, 1.6-liter four with the manual, roughly 126k miles. Not much heat this winter. All the front vents blow barely warm air on both sides, and it's worse at idle. Engine temperature looks normal on the gauge. Separately, the brake pedal feels soft and spongy and goes closer to the floor than it used to, even on the first stop of the day. No warning lights, and no recent brake work. Where do I start?

reply: [SM-7940] Brake fluid moisture test. Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2020. Test the fluid in the reservoir with a brake fluid tester or test strip. Fluid with more than 3 percent water has a reduced boiling point and can vaporize in the calipers, producing a soft pedal. Fluid that is dark or cloudy also indicates contamination. Take the sample before any fluid is added.

snippets.title: Weak heat in cold weather from a thermostat stuck open
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.4L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Heater output may be weak, even with a normal temperature gauge, when the thermostat sticks partly open. From a cold start, idle the engine and watch coolant temperature on a scan tool while feeling the upper radiator hose. It should stay cool until about 195 deg F. Repair: replace the thermostat and gasket.

messages.content: I have a 2015 midsize sedan with the 2.5L four-cylinder and the auto trans, about 184,472 miles. The car pulls hard to the left when I brake. It tracks straight when I'm just driving and when I accelerate. What should I check first?
Thanks for the details. With the front wheels raised, have a helper press and release the brake pedal and spin each front wheel right away to see whether either one stays dragged [SM-3526].
Did that. Both front wheels spin freely right after the pedal is released.
Thanks, that helps narrow it down. Remove the front calipers from their brackets and confirm each slide pin moves freely through its full travel without binding [SB 15-559].
Pulled the pins on both calipers. Clean and they move fine. Nothing found again. I'm ordering a brake hose unless you tell me otherwise.

reply: Measure each front rotor face with an infrared thermometer after a test drive with several moderate stops, park without using the parking brake and take both readings within a minute of stopping; the two should be within about 50 deg F side to side [SM 8.7.8]. A large difference shows which side is braking harder or dragging, and this one reading will tell us whether the heat is coming from the left or right.
